Slopes and gradients

How much does the output move when you nudge the input?

Training adjusts the numbers called weights in a model so that its error, the loss, gets smaller; the slope of the loss with respect to a weight shows which small change of that weight lowers it. This chapter measures a slope by nudging the input, then covers many weights (the gradient), chained functions (the chain rule) and curvature, the slope of the slope. It needs no limits or integrals.

You will need: functions, exponents and logarithms (chapter 0.3), and for the gradient section vectors and dot products (chapter 0.5).

Slope as sensitivity

Guess first. Two made-up sharks, of 80 cm and 50 cm, both grow by 1 cm, and weight is proportional to the cube of length. Does the longer shark gain about the same weight as the shorter one, about 1.5 times as much, or about 2.5 times as much?

Slope is rise divided by run. It is the same at all points of a straight line, but a curve bends, so its slope depends on the point. To measure the slope at \(x\), we nudge the input by a small amount \(h\), the run, and divide the change of the output, the rise, by \(h\). As \(h\) shrinks, this ratio approaches the derivative \(f'(x)\), and the tangent is the straight line through the point with slope \(f'(x)\). In the figure \(x\) is a shark's length \(L\) in cm and \(f(x)\) its weight \(W\) in kg, by the made-up law \(W = 4\times10^{-6}L^3\).

  1. Set the Position slider to 50 and then to 80: the slope in the lower panel rises from 0.0300 to 0.0768.
  2. At 80 cm the shaded triangle shows the nudge, run \(h\) in navy and rise in coral. With \(h = 1\) its dashed side, the chord, lies almost on the teal tangent, and with \(h = 30\) it tilts away.
Curve
Position 0Value 0Slope by the rule 0

The slope is 0.0768 kg per cm at 80 cm and 0.03 at 50 cm, a ratio of 2.56, so the longer shark gains about 2.5 times as much.

How it works

Take the 80 cm shark and nudge its length by 1 cm, so \(h = 1\). The weight rises from \(W(80) = 4\times10^{-6}\times80^3 = 2.048\) kg to \(W(81) = 2.1258\) kg, a rise of 0.0778 kg, so rise divided by run is 0.0778 (kg per cm). For the 50 cm shark \(W(50) = 0.5\) kg and \(W(51) = 0.5306\) kg, a rise of 0.0306 kg, and \(0.0778/0.0306\) is about 2.5, the answer to the guess.

…rise: f(x+h) − f(x)÷…run: the nudge h=…slope of the chord≈…slope by the rule

The slope by the rule comes from the power rule of the next section: the slope of \(4\times10^{-6}L^3\) is \(3\times4\times10^{-6}L^2 = 1.2\times10^{-5}L^2\), which gives 0.0768 at \(L = 80\). As \(h\) shrinks, the chord slope approaches it, for example 0.0868 at \(h = 10\) and 0.0778 at \(h = 1\), because a short piece of a smooth curve is nearly straight. Rearranged, the equation predicts the output after a nudge: \(f(x+h) \approx f(x) + f'(x)\,h\), the old output plus the slope times the nudge. With Position 80 and Nudge \(h\) set to 1, the box shows 0.0778 and 0.0768.

Common belief. A curve has one slope, like a line.

Why it fails. This curve has no single slope: at 80 cm its slope is 2.56 times its slope at 50 cm.

Better account. The derivative is a function that takes a position and returns the slope there.

Quick quiz

What does a derivative of 0.03 kg per cm mean for a shark of 50 cm?

A small nudge of the length adds about 0.03 kg per centimetre of nudge, so growing by 1 cm adds about 30 g. This is accurate when the nudge is small.

Why does the chord slope change when you change the nudge \(h\)?

The chord joins two points on the curve, and a bigger gap lets the curve bend away from the tangent. For a tiny \(h\) the curve looks straight and the chord matches the tangent.

Reading the figure

Drag the coral dot along the curve, or use the slider. The lower panel plots the slope at all positions, so you can see where the curve is steep.

Nudges and limits

Make the nudge large and the chord tilts away from the tangent. Make it small and the two nearly agree. Mathematicians define this with limits. In this primer a nudge small enough that the curve looks straight is enough.

Symbols

\[ f'(x) \approx \frac{f(x+h) - f(x)}{h} \qquad\text{so}\qquad f(x+h) \approx f(x) + f'(x)\,h \]

  • \(f(x)\) is the output of the function at input \(x\). Here \(x\) is a length and \(f(x)\) a weight.
  • \(f'(x)\), read "f prime of x", is the slope at \(x\), also written \(df/dx\). It is itself a function: give it an \(x\), it returns a slope.
  • \(h\) is the nudge. The sign \(\approx\) means "close to, when \(h\) is small".

Forecasts with the slope

The second form of the equation is the one that predicts. At 80 cm the slope is 0.0768 kg per cm, so a shark that grows 2 cm gains about \(2 \times 0.0768 = 0.154\) kg. The true gain is 0.157 kg. The prediction is a little low because the slope keeps rising during the 2 cm.

A second forecast, at 50 cm. The slope is \(1.2\times10^{-5}\times 2500 = 0.03\) kg per cm, so 2 cm of growth should add about 0.06 kg. The true gain is \(4\times10^{-6}(52^3-50^3) = 0.0624\) kg, which is 4% more. For this curve the forecast is low by about \(h/L\): 2.5% at 80 cm and 4% at 50 cm. The slope predicts well for tiny nudges only, and the forecast error grows as the nudge grows relative to \(L\).

The rule for powers

Where does the rule for powers come from? Nudge \(L\) by \(h\) in \(W = 4\times10^{-6}L^3\). Expanding \((L+h)^3 = L^3 + 3L^2h + 3Lh^2 + h^3\) shows that the rise is \(4\times10^{-6}(3L^2h + 3Lh^2 + h^3)\). Divide by \(h\) and the chord slope is \(4\times10^{-6}(3L^2 + 3Lh + h^2)\). As \(h\) shrinks, the last two terms tend to 0 and \(1.2\times10^{-5}L^2\) remains. At 80 cm with \(h=1\) the chord slope is \(4\times10^{-6}\times(19{,}200 + 240 + 1) = 0.0778\), a little above the slope of 0.0768.

In practice

Libraries find slopes by rule. A nudge test is still a standard check for a slope you wrote by hand. With 64-bit numbers a nudge near \(10^{-5}\), taken on both sides of the point, works well. Much smaller nudges lose digits to rounding, as the practice problems show.

In Python

# a made-up law, W = 4e-6 * L^3, in kg
def weight(L):
    return 4e-6 * L ** 3

L, h = 80.0, 0.001
by_nudging = (weight(L + h) - weight(L)) / h
by_formula = 1.2e-5 * L ** 2  # the rule for powers: 3 * 4e-6 * L^2
print(round(by_nudging, 4), "kg per cm, by nudging")
print(round(by_formula, 4), "kg per cm, by formula")
print(round(weight(82) - weight(80), 4), "kg gained going from 80 to 82 cm")
print(round(2 * by_formula, 4), "kg predicted by slope times 2 cm")
0.0768 kg per cm, by nudging
0.0768 kg per cm, by formula
0.1575 kg gained going from 80 to 82 cm
0.1536 kg predicted by slope times 2 cm
# the chord slope at 80 cm for a shrinking nudge h (made-up law, kg)
def weight(L):
    return 4e-6 * L ** 3

for h in [10, 1, 0.1, 0.001]:
    chord = (weight(80 + h) - weight(80)) / h
    print(f"h = {h}: chord slope {chord:.4f}")
print("slope at 50 cm:", round(1.2e-5 * 50 ** 2, 4))
print("gain from 50 to 52 cm:", round(weight(52) - weight(50), 4),
      "against slope times 2:", round(2 * 1.2e-5 * 50 ** 2, 4))
h = 10: chord slope 0.0868
h = 1: chord slope 0.0778
h = 0.1: chord slope 0.0769
h = 0.001: chord slope 0.0768
slope at 50 cm: 0.03
gain from 50 to 52 cm: 0.0624 against slope times 2: 0.06

Common mistakes

Debug tip. A slope has units: output units per input unit. The values 0.0768 kg per cm and 76.8 g per cm are the same slope. If a slope looks absurdly large or small, check that the input and output use the units you think they do.

Where this is used

Used in: the slope of an error is what gradient descent follows (A2), and the nudge test is the basis of gradient checking (B4).

More questions

What is the slope of the weight law at 100 cm, and how does it compare with the slope at 50 cm?

\(1.2\times10^{-5}\times 100^2 = 0.12\) kg per cm. That is 4 times the slope at 50 cm, because the slope goes with \(L^2\) and doubling \(L\) quadruples it.

The slopes this primer uses

Guess first. The sigmoid curve rises from 0 to 1 and is steepest in the middle. Is its steepest slope 1, 0.5 or 0.25?

A rule is a formula that gives a slope without nudging, here for the sigmoid and ReLU, two functions of an input \(z\) that models use. The sigmoid \(\sigma(z) = 1/(1+e^{-z})\) has the rule \(\sigma'(z) = \sigma(z)\,(1-\sigma(z))\), the product of the output and its distance from 1. These two factors add to 1, and their product is largest when both are 0.5, which gives the slope 0.25. Both are 0.5 at \(z = 0\), where \(e^0 = 1\) and \(\sigma(0) = 1/2\). In the flat tails one factor is close to 0, so the slope is close to 0 and the sigmoid is called saturated. ReLU, \(\mathrm{ReLU}(z) = \max(0, z)\), is the larger of 0 and \(z\), so its slope is 0 for negative \(z\) and 1 for positive \(z\).

  1. Choose Sigmoid. The navy curve is the output \(\sigma(z)\) and the coral curve is its slope. Slide \(z\) to 0: the coral curve peaks at 0.25, the product 0.500 × 0.500 in the box under the plot.
  2. Slide \(z\) to 5: the output is 0.993, almost 1, and the slope falls to 0.0066, because a nudge of \(z\) hardly moves the output in the flat tail.
  3. Choose ReLU: the coral slope is 0 for negative \(z\), 1 for positive \(z\).
Function

The sigmoid's slope peaks at 0.25 at \(z = 0\) and falls to 0.0066 at \(z = 5\), where the curve is almost flat.

How it works

Take \(z = 2\). Here \(e^{-2} = 0.135\), so \(\sigma(2) = 1/(1+0.135) = 0.881\) and \(1-\sigma(2) = 0.119\). The slope is their product, 0.105, less than half of the 0.25 at \(z = 0\).

σ′(2)the slope: 0.105=σ(2)the output: 0.881×1 − σ(2)its distance from 1: 0.119

A product of two numbers with a fixed sum is largest when they are equal, so the slope peaks at \(z = 0\). The worked examples in the next sections use a few other rules. A constant has slope 0, a constant multiple \(c\,g(x)\) of a function \(g\) has slope \(c\,g'(x)\), slopes of sums add, and \(x^n\) has slope \(n\,x^{n-1}\). The Go deeper part below has the whole table, with \(e^x\) and \(\ln x\), and says what happens to ReLU at \(z = 0\).

Common belief. Where the output is large, the slope is large.

Why it fails. A sigmoid output of 0.999 has a slope near 0.001, because the value locates the point on the curve and the slope measures how much a nudge changes the output there.

Better account. Track the value and the slope separately. A saturated sigmoid has an output near 0 or 1 and a slope near 0, so a nudge of \(z\) hardly changes its output.

Quick quiz

What is the sigmoid's slope at \(z = 0\), and why is that its maximum?

It is \(0.5 \times 0.5 = 0.25\). The product \(\sigma(1-\sigma)\) is largest when \(\sigma = 0.5\), and \(\sigma = 0.5\) at \(z = 0\).

A ReLU receives \(z = -3\). What does a nudge of \(z\) do to its output?

The output does not change, because the slope is 0 there: \(\mathrm{ReLU}(-3) = 0\) and it stays 0 for a small nudge. A ReLU that receives a negative score for all inputs gives zero slope to the weights that feed it, a problem called a dead ReLU (the debugging chapter returns to it).

Go deeper table of rules, tanh and ReLU, Python about 4 min

Flat tails and the table

Slide \(z\) to the right and watch the coral slope curve. In the tails the output hardly reacts to a nudge of \(z\). By the chain rule (a later section) the slope of a loss with respect to a weight that contributes to \(z\) contains this small slope as a factor. The product is small when the other factors are not large, as for squared error or for a hidden neuron. The log loss of A3 is the exception at the output, where the factor cancels. B4 and B6 return to this as vanishing gradients. The table lists the rules you will meet. The rows for powers, \(e^{x}\) and \(\ln x\) are the basic rules. The sigmoid row follows from them with the chain rule (exercise 2 does it), and the tanh row follows from the sigmoid row because \(\tanh z = 2\sigma(2z) - 1\).

The table of rules

functionslopeused in
a constant \(c\)\(0\)bias terms drop out of slopes
\(c\,g(x)\)\(c\,g'(x)\)scaling a loss scales its slope
\(g(x) + k(x)\)\(g'(x) + k'(x)\)a total loss is a sum over examples (A2)
\(x^n\)\(n\,x^{n-1}\)the weight law (A2) and squared error (A2)
\(e^{x}\)\(e^{x}\)softmax (0.7)
\(\ln x\)\(1/x\)cross-entropy (0.7)
\(\sigma(z)\)\(\sigma(z)\,(1-\sigma(z))\)logistic regression and neurons (A3, B1)
\(\tanh z\)\(1-\tanh^2 z\)neurons (B1)
\(\mathrm{ReLU}(z)\)\(0\) if \(z<0\), \(1\) if \(z>0\)neurons and backprop (B1, B4)

ReLU has a corner at \(z = 0\), where no single slope exists. Most libraries use 0 there. It usually does not matter, because \(z\) is seldom equal to 0 for measured inputs.

The table in use

Take \(f(x) = 3x^2 + 2\ln x + 5\) at \(x = 2\). The constant 5 drops out, \(3x^2\) has slope \(6x\) and \(2\ln x\) has slope \(2/x\). The slope is \(6\cdot2 + 2/2 = 13\), and a nudge of \(10^{-6}\) gives 13.0000. Now compare activations. Tanh has slope \(1-\tanh^2 z\), which is 1 at \(z=0\) and 0.071 at \(z=2\). The sigmoid has 0.25 and 0.105 at the same points. At its peak the tanh slope is four times the sigmoid's, and it falls off faster in the tails.

Sigmoids in a stack

The peak of 0.25 matters in a stack. With weights near 1, a sigmoid layer multiplies a nudge by at most about a quarter, so ten of them multiply it by at most \(0.25^{10} \approx 10^{-6}\). This is one reason deep networks avoid sigmoids in their hidden layers (B4).

In practice

Deep-learning libraries store one rule per operation and combine them with the chain rule, so you rarely write a slope by hand. You still need the table to explain what training does. ReLU became a common default in hidden layers partly because its slope is 1 when \(z\) is positive, so it does not shrink the slope that is passed back through it.

In Python

import numpy as np

def sigmoid(z):
    return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))

h = 1e-6
for z in [0.0, 2.0, 5.0]:
    nudged = (sigmoid(z + h) - sigmoid(z)) / h
    formula = sigmoid(z) * (1 - sigmoid(z))
    print(f"z = {z}: nudged {nudged:.4f}, formula {formula:.4f}")

relu = lambda z: np.maximum(0, z)
for z in [-2.0, 3.0]:
    print(f"ReLU slope at {z}:", round((relu(z + h) - relu(z)) / h, 3))
z = 0.0: nudged 0.2500, formula 0.2500
z = 2.0: nudged 0.1050, formula 0.1050
z = 5.0: nudged 0.0066, formula 0.0066
ReLU slope at -2.0: 0.0
ReLU slope at 3.0: 1.0
import numpy as np

def f(x):
    return 3 * x ** 2 + 2 * np.log(x) + 5

h = 1e-6
by_rules = 6 * 2 + 2 / 2                # slopes: 6x and 2/x
by_nudging = (f(2 + h) - f(2)) / h
print(by_rules, round(by_nudging, 4))

for z in [0.0, 2.0]:
    sig = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))
    t_slope, s_slope = 1 - np.tanh(z) ** 2, sig * (1 - sig)
    print(f"z = {z}: tanh slope {t_slope:.4f}, sigmoid slope {s_slope:.4f}")
print("ten sigmoid layers, at best:", f"{0.25 ** 10:.2e}")
13.0 13.0
z = 0.0: tanh slope 1.0000, sigmoid slope 0.2500
z = 2.0: tanh slope 0.0707, sigmoid slope 0.1050
ten sigmoid layers, at best: 9.54e-07

Where this is used

Used in: the sigmoid and ReLU slopes feed neurons (B1) and backpropagation (B4); flat tails lead to vanishing gradients (B6).

More questions

What is the slope of \(5x^4\) at \(x = 2\)?

The rule for powers gives \(5\times4x^3 = 20x^3\), which is \(20\times8 = 160\).

Partial derivatives

Guess first. A model has two weights, \(w_1\) and \(w_2\), and a loss \(L\) that depends on both. You nudge only \(w_1\) and keep \(w_2\) fixed. Can the answer to "how fast does \(L\) change?" depend on the value of \(w_2\)?

The weights \(w_1\) and \(w_2\) are the dials of the model. Its loss \(L\) (section 1 used this letter for a length) is one number that measures the model's error, lower being better. Freezing \(w_2\), that is keeping it at a fixed value, leaves \(L\) as a curve in \(w_1\) alone, called a slice. The partial derivative \(\partial L/\partial w_1\) is the ordinary slope of this slice, found by nudging only \(w_1\). The figure draws \(L\) as a contour map, seen from above, where a contour line joins the points that have the same loss.

  1. The navy line is the slice with \(w_2\) frozen, drawn with its tangent in the top small plot, and the sand line is the slice with \(w_1\) frozen, drawn in the lower one. Set \(w_1 = 2\) and \(w_2 = 1\) with the sliders: the slopes are 2.40 in the top plot and 3.90 in the lower plot.
  2. Now set \(w_2 = -0.5\) and keep \(w_1 = 2\). The slope in the top plot falls to 1.50, although \(w_1\) did not move.

Click the contour map to move the point.

At \(w_1 = 2\) the slope along \(w_1\) is 2.40 with \(w_2 = 1\) and 1.50 with \(w_2 = -0.5\), so for this loss the answer to the guess is yes.

How it works

Take the made-up loss of the figure, which the next section calls the bowl: \(L = 0.5u^2 + v^2 + 0.6uv\), where \(u = w_1-0.5\) and \(v = w_2+0.5\). A change of \(w_1\) changes \(u\) by the same amount, and freezing \(w_2 = 1\) makes \(v = 1.5\). Then \(v^2 = 2.25\) and \(0.6uv = 0.9u\), so \(L = 0.5u^2 + 0.9u + 2.25\), a curve in \(w_1\) alone. The rules of the previous section give its slope \(u + 0.9\), which is 2.4 at \(w_1 = 2\), where \(u = 1.5\). Freezing \(w_2 = -0.5\) makes \(v = 0\), so \(L = 0.5u^2\) and the slope at \(w_1 = 2\) is \(u = 1.5\).

…∂L/∂w1: slope along w1and…∂L/∂w2: slope along w2at…(w1, w2)

The curly \(\partial\) means that the other weight is frozen while this one is nudged: \(\partial L/\partial w_1 \approx \bigl(L(w_1+h,\,w_2)-L(w_1,\,w_2)\bigr)/h\). Here \(\partial L/\partial w_1 = u + 0.6v\), so the slope along \(w_1\) depends on \(w_2\) through \(v\), because the cross term \(0.6uv\) links the two weights. Set \(w_1 = 2\) and \(w_2 = 1\) and the box shows 2.40 and 3.90.

Analogy. Think of the loss as the height of a hillside, seen from above in the map, with east as \(w_1\) and north as \(w_2\). The slope towards the east and the slope towards the north are two different numbers, and walking along one compass direction measures one of them, as freezing the other weight does.

Where it breaks. A hillside has two directions to check, but a model can have millions of weights and so millions of partial derivatives, and you cannot draw that hill. The idea extends to any number of weights, and the picture does not.

Quick quiz

What does the symbol \(\partial L/\partial w_2\) ask you to do?

Nudge \(w_2\), keep \(w_1\) frozen, and measure how much \(L\) changes per unit nudge.

For \(L = 3w_1^2 + w_1w_2\), what is \(\partial L/\partial w_2\)?

Freeze \(w_1\). The term \(3w_1^2\) is a constant and drops out, and \(w_1w_2\) has slope \(w_1\). So \(\partial L/\partial w_2 = w_1\).

Go deeper map reading, symbols, backpropagation cost, Python about 2 min

Reading the figure

The map is a view from above, like a hill drawn with contour lines. The numbers on the contour lines give the loss. The horizontal navy line is the slice where \(w_2\) is frozen; the sand vertical line is the slice where \(w_1\) is frozen. Both slices appear on the right as ordinary curves with ordinary tangents. Move the point up and down: the top-right curve shifts and its slope changes, even though you never touched \(w_1\). The partial derivative depends on where all the weights are, including the ones you did not nudge.

Symbols

\[ \frac{\partial L}{\partial w_1} \approx \frac{L(w_1 + h,\; w_2) - L(w_1,\; w_2)}{h} \qquad \frac{\partial L}{\partial w_2} \approx \frac{L(w_1,\; w_2 + h) - L(w_1,\; w_2)}{h} \]

  • \(\partial\) is a curly "d". It says other variables are frozen while this one is nudged.
  • \(L(w_1 + h,\; w_2)\) is the loss after nudging only \(w_1\).

In practice

A model with a million weights has a million partial derivatives. Nudging the weights one at a time would cost a million evaluations of the loss. Backpropagation (B4) gets all of them from one forward and one backward pass, at a cost of a few forward passes. That is one reason training large networks is practical.

In Python

def L(w1, w2):
    a, b = w1 - 0.5, w2 + 0.5
    return 0.5 * a ** 2 + b ** 2 + 0.6 * a * b

h = 1e-6
for w2 in [1.0, -0.5]:
    slope = (L(2 + h, w2) - L(2 - h, w2)) / (2 * h)     # nudge w1 only
    print(f"w2 frozen at {w2}: slope along w1 = {slope:.3f}")
w2 frozen at 1.0: slope along w1 = 2.400
w2 frozen at -0.5: slope along w1 = 1.500

Common mistakes

Debug tip. If a hand-written derivative disagrees with a nudge test, check which variable you nudged. Swapping \(w_1\) and \(w_2\) in a formula gives a plausible but wrong answer.

Where this is used

Used in: a model has one partial derivative per weight, which together form the gradient in the next section (A2, B3).

More questions

On the map, where is a slice with \(w_2\) frozen?

It is a horizontal line through the point, because \(w_2\) is the vertical axis and stays fixed along it.

The gradient

Guess first. You are on a foggy hillside and can feel only the slope under your feet: +2 (uphill) towards the east and +3 (uphill) towards the north. In which direction does the ground rise fastest, east, north or somewhere between, and how steep is it there?

The gradient \(\nabla L\) is the vector of all the partial derivatives, here \((\partial L/\partial w_1,\ \partial L/\partial w_2)\). At a point it points in the direction in which the loss rises fastest, it crosses the contour line at right angles, and its length is the slope in that direction. The hillside of the guess has gradient \((2, 3)\), so the ground rises fastest between east and north, with slope \(\sqrt{2^2+3^2} \approx 3.6\). Minus the gradient points downhill, the direction of steepest descent, and a downhill step with step size \(\eta\), also called the learning rate, changes the weights \(\mathbf{w}\) to \(\mathbf{w} - \eta\,\nabla L\).

  1. The coral arrow at the point is the gradient and the teal arrow is minus the gradient, and both cross the contour line at a right angle.
  2. On the Bowl press "Step downhill" once: the point moves along the teal arrow and the loss falls from 5.06 to 0.543. Choose "Narrow valley" and press it several times: the points zig-zag across the valley.
Surface

Drag the 3D view to rotate it. Click the contour map to move the point.

The coral arrow is the gradient: it crosses the contour line at a right angle and points to higher loss. The teal arrow, minus the gradient, points downhill.

How it works

Take the gradient \((2, 3)\) of the guess. A step of \((a, b)\) rises \(2a + 3b\), so a unit step east rises 2 and a unit step north rises 3. A unit step along the gradient, \((2,3)/\sqrt{13} = (0.555,\ 0.832)\), rises \(2\times0.555 + 3\times0.832 = 3.6\), more than either. This rise is the length \(\sqrt{13} = 3.6\) of the gradient, and the direction is 56 degrees above east, the angle whose tangent is \(3/2\).

…∂L/∂w1,…∂L/∂w2→…length of the gradient: the steepness,…loss at the point

The slope in the direction of a unit vector \(\mathbf{u}\), a vector of length 1, is the dot product \(\nabla L\cdot\mathbf{u}\). For vectors of fixed length a dot product is largest when they point the same way, and then it equals the length of the gradient. So the gradient gives the steepest direction, and its length is \(\|\nabla L\| = \sqrt{(\partial L/\partial w_1)^2 + (\partial L/\partial w_2)^2}\). Set \(w_1 = 1.85\) and \(w_2 = 0.60\) and the box shows about \((2.01,\ 3.01)\), length 3.62, close to the gradient \((2, 3)\) of the guess.

Common belief. Minus the gradient points at the minimum.

Why it fails. Minus the gradient gives the steepest downhill direction at the current point only, and in the narrow valley that direction points mostly across the valley, so repeated steps zig-zag.

Better account. The gradient is a local direction, so take a small step and then compute the gradient again.

Quick quiz

The gradient at a point is (3, 4). How steep is the steepest direction, and which way is downhill?

The steepness is \(\sqrt{9+16} = 5\). Downhill is the opposite direction, \((-3, -4)\).

The loss is \(w_1^2 + w_2^2\). What is the gradient at \((3,4)\), and where does a step with \(\eta = 0.1\) take the point?

The partial derivatives are \(2w_1 = 6\) and \(2w_2 = 8\), so the gradient is \((6,8)\), with length 10. The step moves to \((3-0.6,\ 4-0.8) = (2.4,\ 3.2)\).

Go deeper symbols, zero gradients, nudge check, Python about 4 min

Reading the figure

Rotate the left view to see the surface from the side. The right view is the same surface from above. Switch on the arrow field to see the gradient at many points. Arrow lengths grow with the steepness but are limited for display, so the box below the plot gives the true steepness. Where the gradient is not zero, the arrows cross the contour lines at right angles. Press "Step downhill" to move the point by \(\eta\) times the gradient, against it. On the bowl, a press lowers the loss. Try the narrow valley: the steps zig-zag across the valley instead of running along it.

Symbols

\[ \nabla L = \left(\frac{\partial L}{\partial w_1},\; \frac{\partial L}{\partial w_2}\right) \qquad \|\nabla L\| = \sqrt{\left(\frac{\partial L}{\partial w_1}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{\partial L}{\partial w_2}\right)^2} \qquad \mathbf{w} \leftarrow \mathbf{w} - \eta\,\nabla L \]

  • \(\nabla L\), read "grad L" or "nabla L", lists one partial derivative per weight. With a million weights it has a million entries.
  • \(\|\nabla L\|\) is its length, the slope in the steepest direction. For a gradient \((2, 3)\) it is \(\sqrt{13} \approx 3.6\), the answer to the guess.
  • \(\mathbf{w} \leftarrow \mathbf{w} - \eta\,\nabla L\) is the downhill step the button takes. A2 turns it into training.

Points where the gradient is zero

The gradient is zero at the bottom of the bowl, and the loss is flat there. Choose the saddle or the two dips and find other points where the gradient is zero but you are not at a lowest point. The curvature section at the end of the chapter tells a valley bottom from a hilltop or a saddle. Comparing the loss at the two dips tells the higher one from the lower one.

In Python

import numpy as np

def L(w):  # a tilted bowl, lowest at (0.5, -0.5)
    a, b = w[0] - 0.5, w[1] + 0.5
    return 0.5 * a**2 + 1.0 * b**2 + 0.6 * a * b

def grad(w):  # the two partial derivatives, by rule
    a, b = w[0] - 0.5, w[1] + 0.5
    return np.array([a + 0.6 * b, 2 * b + 0.6 * a])

def grad_by_nudging(w, h=1e-5):
    g = np.zeros_like(w)
    for j in range(len(w)):  # nudge one weight, freeze the others
        step = np.zeros_like(w)
        step[j] = h
        g[j] = (L(w + step) - L(w - step)) / (2 * h)
    return g

w = np.array([2.0, 1.0])
print("rule    :", grad(w))
print("nudging :", np.round(grad_by_nudging(w), 4))
print("loss now:", L(w))
print("after one step of 0.3 downhill:", round(L(w - 0.3 * grad(w)), 4))

for step in range(4):  # four steps of size 0.3, always downhill
    print(step, w.round(3), round(L(w), 4))
    w = w - 0.3 * grad(w)
rule    : [2.4 3.9]
nudging : [2.4 3.9]
loss now: 4.725
after one step of 0.3 downhill: 0.5675
0 [2. 1.] 4.725
1 [ 1.28 -0.17] 0.5675
2 [ 0.987 -0.508] 0.116
3 [ 0.842 -0.591] 0.0481

Follow the printed steps. From \((2,1)\) the gradient is \((2.4,\ 3.9)\), so a step of 0.3 moves the point to \((2-0.72,\ 1-1.17) = (1.28,\ -0.17)\). The loss falls from 4.725 to 0.5675. There the gradient is \((0.978,\ 1.128)\), much smaller, so the next step is shorter and ends at \((0.987,\ -0.508)\). The steps get shorter because the gradient is smaller near the bottom.

Checking a gradient by nudging

The nudge uses both sides of the point (\(L(w+h) - L(w-h)\), divided by \(2h\)). That is more accurate than nudging one side. B4 uses this same check to test a backpropagation implementation.

In practice

A gradient with a million entries is rarely printed. People watch its length, called the gradient norm (B8), and the loss. A loss measured on a small batch gives a noisy gradient (B3). A single step may then fail to lower the loss even when the code is right.

Common mistakes

Debug tip. A gradient has one entry per weight. If its size differs from the size of the weights, or a very small step along minus the gradient raises the loss, the gradient code is probably wrong. The nudge test in the code above catches both.

Where this is used

Used in: one gradient entry per weight is what training computes (A2, B3), and the loss surface idea returns in B3.

More questions

A contour line runs north-east at the point. Which way does the gradient point?

At right angles to it: north-west or south-east, whichever side has higher loss.

The chain rule

Guess first. A made-up neuron in SharkCam, the shark-spotting robot, computes a score \(z = 0.1\,(x - 70)\) from a length \(x\) in cm. It then computes \(a = \sigma(z)\), its probability that the shark is an adult, with \(\sigma\) the sigmoid. You nudge \(x\) by 1 cm, which moves \(z\) by 0.1, and at \(x = 78\) cm the sigmoid has a slope of about 0.21. By roughly how much does \(a\) move?

A chain of functions feeds the output of one into the next, here \(x \to z \to a\) (a composition). A small nudge of \(x\) is multiplied by the local slopes of the links it goes through. The local slope of a link is the slope of its output with respect to its input, at the value the link receives now. So the slope of the whole chain is the product of the local slopes, which is the chain rule: \(da/dx = (da/dz)(dz/dx)\).

  1. With the defaults (\(x = 78\) cm, \(\Delta x = 1\) cm) press "Nudge". The change in \(z\) is 0.100 and in \(a\) 0.0210. The boxes under the tracks multiply the nudge by the slopes 0.1000 and 0.2139 to predict 0.0214, close to 0.0210.
  2. Set \(\Delta x\) to 20 cm. The product of slopes stays 0.0214, but the actual change divided by \(\Delta x\) falls to 0.0126, so the gap grows from 0.0004 to 0.0088.
Chain

A 1 cm nudge in \(x\) becomes 0.1 in \(z\) and about 0.021 in \(a\), so the slope of the chain is \(0.1 \times 0.214 = 0.0214\), which answers the guess: about 0.02.

How it works

Take \(x = 78\). Then \(z = 0.1\,(78-70) = 0.8\), \(a = 1/(1+e^{-0.8}) = 0.690\), and the local slope of the sigmoid is \(0.690\times0.310 = 0.214\), while the local slope of the score is 0.1. Their product is 0.0214, so a 1 cm nudge raises \(a\) by about 0.021.

da/dxslope of the chain: 0.0214=da/dzlocal slope of σ at z = 0.8: 0.214×dz/dxlocal slope of the score: 0.1

The rule follows from using the nudge idea twice: a nudge \(\Delta x\) moves \(z\) by about \((dz/dx)\,\Delta x\), and that change moves \(a\) by about \(da/dz\) times as much, so \(\Delta a \approx (da/dz)(dz/dx)\,\Delta x\). The local slopes are measured at the starting point, so the rule is accurate while they stay nearly constant, that is, for small nudges. From 78 cm, a growth of 10 cm is forecast to raise \(a\) by \(10\times0.0214 = 0.214\), but the true rise is \(0.858-0.690 = 0.168\), since the slope falls as the sigmoid flattens.

Analogy. In a train of two gear pairs, the first makes its output shaft turn 10 times as fast as its input and the second 4 times as fast. The last shaft then turns 40 times as fast as the first, because the factors multiply. These factors play the part of the local slopes.

Where it breaks. A gear factor is fixed, but a local slope depends on where the signal is now.

Quick quiz

The local slopes along a chain are 3, 0.5 and 0.1. What is the slope of the whole chain?

\(3 \times 0.5 \times 0.1 = 0.15\).

Why can the chain rule fail for a large nudge?

A local slope is measured at the starting point. A large nudge moves the signal to where the slopes are different, so the product no longer matches the true change.

Go deeper symbols, other lengths, large inputs, Python about 4 min

Reading the figure

Press "Nudge" to watch the change travel down the chain. The top slider moves by \(\Delta x\). The link below it multiplies the change by its local slope, so the second slider moves by \(0.1\,\Delta x\), and the link below that multiplies again. Use the two controls to move the starting point and to enlarge the nudge. A large nudge breaks the match between the product of slopes and the actual change, because the slopes change along the way. Add the loss link to see a longer chain.

Symbols

\[ \frac{da}{dx} = \frac{da}{dz}\cdot\frac{dz}{dx} \qquad\qquad \frac{d\ell}{dw} = \frac{d\ell}{da}\cdot\frac{da}{dz}\cdot\frac{dz}{dw} \]

  • \(x \to z \to a\) is a chain: \(z = wx + b\) is a weighted sum and \(a = \sigma(z)\) is the neuron's output.
  • \(\ell\) is the loss for one example, here \((a - y)^2\) for a label \(y\).
  • In training you nudge the weight \(w\), not the input. The chain is the same, with \(dz/dw = x\) as the first link.

The same nudge at other lengths

The same 1 cm matters differently at other lengths. At \(x=60\) cm, \(z=-1\), the sigmoid slope is 0.197 and the chain slope is \(0.1\times0.197 = 0.0197\). At 78 cm it is 0.0214. At 90 cm, \(z=2\), it is \(0.1\times0.105 = 0.0105\). At 120 cm, \(z=5\), it is 0.00066. A 120 cm shark moves the output more than 30 times less per centimetre than a 78 cm one, because the sigmoid is saturated there. The larger nudge of 10 cm from 78 cm is worked in the layers above: the forecast is 0.214 and the true rise 0.168.

A weight attached to a large input

The last local slope, \(dz/dw = 78\), is large because lengths are in centimetres. A weight attached to a big input changes the score by a large amount, which makes its gradient large. This is one reason A2 rescales features before training.

In practice

Libraries keep \(z\) and \(a\) from the forward pass, because the local slopes need them. This is part of why training uses more memory than prediction.

In Python

import numpy as np

def sigmoid(z):
    return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))

x, y = 78.0, 1.0  # a 78 cm shark, label 1 = adult
def loss(w, b=-7.0):
    z = w * x + b  # score
    a = sigmoid(z)  # probability of adult
    return (a - y) ** 2

w = 0.1
z = w * x - 7.0
a = sigmoid(z)
dl_da = 2 * (a - y)  # slope of the loss with respect to a
da_dz = a * (1 - a)  # slope of the sigmoid
dz_dw = x  # z = w*x + b, so nudging w moves z by x
chain = dl_da * da_dz * dz_dw
nudge = (loss(w + 1e-6) - loss(w)) / 1e-6

print("local slopes:", round(dl_da, 4), round(da_dz, 4), dz_dw)
print("chain rule  :", round(chain, 4))
print("by nudging  :", round(nudge, 4))
local slopes: -0.6201 0.2139 78.0
chain rule  : -10.3455
by nudging  : -10.3451
import numpy as np

def sigmoid(z):
    return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))

def a_of(x):
    return sigmoid(0.1 * (x - 70))      # length x -> score z -> probability a

for x in [60, 78, 90, 120]:
    a = a_of(x)
    chain = 0.1 * a * (1 - a)           # dz/dx times da/dz
    true = a_of(x + 1) - a              # the true change for a 1 cm nudge
    print(f"x = {x}: chain slope {chain:.5f}, true change {true:.5f}")
forecast = 10 * 0.1 * sigmoid(0.8) * (1 - sigmoid(0.8))
true_rise = a_of(88) - a_of(78)
print("10 cm from 78: forecast", round(forecast, 3), "true", round(true_rise, 3))
x = 60: chain slope 0.01966, true change 0.02011
x = 78: chain slope 0.02139, true change 0.02098
x = 90: chain slope 0.01050, true change 0.01011
x = 120: chain slope 0.00066, true change 0.00063
10 cm from 78: forecast 0.214 true 0.168

Common mistakes

Debug tip. A product with one near-zero factor is near zero. If the gradient at a weight is tiny, list the local slopes along its chain. A saturated sigmoid (slope 0.001) or a ReLU receiving a negative score (slope 0) is a common cause (B8).

Where this is used

B4 builds this into backpropagation: it walks the chain from the loss back to the weights and multiplies the local slopes on the way, once for all the weights.

Used in: backpropagation multiplies local slopes along a computation graph (B4).

More questions

One link of a chain has slope 0, such as a ReLU that received a negative score. What is the slope of the whole chain?

It is 0, whatever the other links are. A product with a zero factor is zero, so no nudge of the input reaches the output.

Curvature: the slope of the slope

Guess first. Two valleys share their lowest point, and their curvature, larger for a sharper bend, is 6 in the sharp valley and 0.5 in the flat valley. You move a weight 0.5 from the bottom in both: how many times more does the loss rise in the sharp valley, 6, 12 or 144 times?

The second derivative \(f''(x)\) is the slope of the slope, and its value \(k\) is the curvature. At a small distance \(\delta\) from the bottom of a smooth valley the loss has risen by about \(\tfrac12 k\,\delta^2\). At the same distance the rise is proportional to \(k\), so it is \(6/0.5 = 12\) times as large in the sharp valley. For step size \(\eta\), a gradient step turns the distance \(\delta\) into about \((1-\eta k)\,\delta\), so the same \(\eta\) gives slow progress in the flat valley and can bounce across the sharp one.

  1. Coral is the sharp valley, navy the flat valley. Press "Take 8 steps" with \(\eta = 0.25\): the walker, the point that takes the steps, bounces across the bottom in the sharp valley and ends close to it, but creeps from one side in the flat valley.
  2. Raise \(\eta\) to 0.4 and press again: the sharp walker bounces further out step after step, and the flat walker moves faster.

At 0.5 from the bottom the sharp valley has 12 times the loss rise of the flat one; at step size 0.25 its walker bounces, the flat one creeps.

How it works

Take \(\delta = 0.5\). The sharp valley (\(k = 6\)) has a loss rise of \(\tfrac12\times6\times0.5^2 = 0.75\) and the flat valley (\(k = 0.5\)) of \(\tfrac12\times0.5\times0.5^2 = 0.0625\), a ratio of 12. With \(\eta = 0.25\), one step multiplies the distance by \(1-0.25\times6 = -0.5\) in the sharp valley, so the walker crosses the bottom to a negative distance, and by \(1-0.25\times0.5 = 0.875\) in the flat valley.

(1 − ηk) δthe distance after one step=−0.25sharp valley: −0.5 × 0.5and0.4375flat valley: 0.875 × 0.5

Near the bottom \(w^\ast\) the slope \(f'\) is 0, so the loss is about \(f(w^\ast) + \tfrac12 k\,\delta^2\). The slope of this parabola is \(k\delta\), so a step of size \(\eta\) turns \(\delta\) into \(\delta - \eta k\delta = (1-\eta k)\,\delta\). The distance shrinks in size when \(0 < \eta k < 2\), that is, when \(\eta < 2/k\), and the walker crosses the bottom when \(\eta k > 1\).

Common belief. If the gradient is zero, training has found the lowest point.

Why it fails. A zero gradient also occurs at a hilltop, at a saddle (up in one direction, down in another) and at a valley bottom that is higher than another one. Curvature is positive at a valley bottom that curves and negative at a hilltop.

Better account. The gradient gives a direction to move. Near a valley bottom the curvature \(k\) limits the step size that keeps the distance from growing, \(\eta \le 2/k\); with many weights the largest curvature sets the limit.

Quick quiz

A valley has curvature 4. How much does the loss rise when you move 0.3 from the bottom?

\(\tfrac12 \times 4 \times 0.3^2 = 0.18\).

For curvature 10, what is the largest step size that does not make the distance to the bottom grow?

\(2/10 = 0.2\). Above it, a gradient step overshoots by more than the distance it started from.

Go deeper Hessian, symbols, derivations, Python about 5 min

Reading the figure

Slide the distance \(\delta\) from the bottom. Then press "Take 8 steps" to start from \(\delta\) and walk downhill with step size \(\eta\) in both valleys. When \(\eta k\) is between 1 and 2 the walker overshoots the bottom and bounces across it, still getting closer. Above 2 it bounces further out at the next step.

Symbols

\[ f''(x) \approx \frac{f(x+h) - 2f(x) + f(x-h)}{h^2} \qquad f(w^\ast + \delta) \approx f(w^\ast) + \tfrac{1}{2}\,f''(w^\ast)\,\delta^2 \qquad \eta < \frac{2}{k} \]

  • \(f''(x)\) is the second derivative, the slope of the slope. The first formula estimates it from the values of \(f\) at \(x-h\), \(x\) and \(x+h\).
  • \(w^\ast\) is the lowest point and \(\delta\) the distance from it. The middle formula says the loss rises like \(\tfrac12 k\delta^2\) with \(k = f''\).
  • \(\eta < 2/k\) is the condition for a gradient step to shrink the distance, for a perfect parabola of curvature \(k\). At \(\eta = 2/k\) the distance keeps its size and the walker bounces between two points.

Two steps behind these formulas

Near a smooth bottom the loss is about \(f(w^\ast) + f'(w^\ast)\delta + \tfrac12 f''(w^\ast)\delta^2\), the second-order Taylor expansion. The slope \(f'\) is 0 at the bottom, so the middle term vanishes and \(\tfrac12 k\delta^2\) is the first term left. For that parabola the slope is \(k\delta\), so one step of size \(\eta\) gives a new distance \(\delta - \eta k\delta = (1-\eta k)\delta\). The distance shrinks when \(\lvert 1-\eta k\rvert < 1\), which means \(0 < \eta k < 2\).

Many weights: the Hessian

With many weights, curvature is a table of second partial derivatives, the Hessian. Its eigenvectors (0.5) are the directions in which the valley is sharpest and flattest, and its eigenvalues are the curvatures along them. A saddle has positive curvature in one direction and negative in another: the gradient is zero there, yet it is no minimum. Positive curvature means a valley, negative means a hilltop.

A two-weight case

The bowl of the last section has second derivatives 1 along \(w_1\), 2 along \(w_2\) and 0.6 for the mixed term, so the Hessian is \(\begin{pmatrix}1&0.6\\0.6&2\end{pmatrix}\). The trace is 3 and the determinant is \(2-0.36 = 1.64\), so \(\lambda^2-3\lambda+1.64=0\) and \(\lambda = (3\pm\sqrt{2.44})/2 = 2.281\) or \(0.719\). The sharpest direction has curvature 2.28, so the largest safe step is \(2/2.281 = 0.877\). The code runs 60 steps at 0.8 and at 0.9.

import numpy as np

H = np.array([[1.0, 0.6],
              [0.6, 2.0]])               # second derivatives of the bowl
vals, vecs = np.linalg.eigh(H)
limit = 2 / vals.max()
print("curvatures:", vals.round(3), " step limit 2/max:", round(limit, 3))

def grad(w):                              # gradient of the bowl
    a, b = w[0] - 0.5, w[1] + 0.5
    return np.array([a + 0.6 * b, 2 * b + 0.6 * a])

for eta in [0.8, 0.9]:
    w = np.array([2.0, 1.0])
    for _ in range(60):
        w = w - eta * grad(w)
    dist = np.linalg.norm(w - [0.5, -0.5])
    print(f"eta = {eta}: distance from the bottom after 60 steps = {dist:.5f}")
curvatures: [0.719 2.281]  step limit 2/max: 0.877
eta = 0.8: distance from the bottom after 60 steps = 0.00002
eta = 0.9: distance from the bottom after 60 steps = 44.01931

Along the sharpest direction a step multiplies the distance by \(1-\eta\lambda\). At 0.8 that factor is \(-0.82\), so the distance shrinks. At 0.9 it is \(-1.05\), so the distance grows by about 5% per step and the walker moves away from the bottom.

Where curvature returns

Curvature appears again in the optimiser chapter (B5), where Adam's running average of squared gradients is often read as a rough gauge of curvature, though that chapter shows where the reading fails. It also returns in B7: when the model's probabilities are close to the truth, the Fisher information is close to the curvature of the loss, and a weight with a large Fisher information is costly to change under the penalty described there.

In Python

# a valley with its bottom at w = 0
def f(w, k):
    return 0.5 * k * w ** 2

def second_derivative(f, w, k, h=1e-3):
    return (f(w + h, k) - 2 * f(w, k) + f(w - h, k)) / h ** 2

for name, k in [("sharp", 6.0), ("flat", 0.5)]:
    curv = second_derivative(f, 0.5, k)
    rise = f(0.5, k)
    w = 1.5
    for _ in range(8):  # eight gradient steps, step size 0.25
        w = w - 0.25 * (k * w)
    print(f"{name}: curvature {curv:.2f}, loss rise at 0.5 = {rise:.3f}, w after 8 steps = {w:.3f}")
sharp: curvature 6.00, loss rise at 0.5 = 0.750, w after 8 steps = 0.006
flat: curvature 0.50, loss rise at 0.5 = 0.062, w after 8 steps = 0.515

Both walkers started at 1.5. The sharp one bounced from side to side (the factor is \(1 - 0.25 \times 6 = -0.5\)) and ended near the bottom. The flat one shrank its distance by only 12.5% per step.

Common mistakes

Debug tip. If the loss swings up and down between two values, or grows without bound, the step size is probably too large for the curvature. Halve the learning rate first and see whether the swing calms down.

In practice

The full Hessian of a large network is rarely formed, since a million weights give a table of \(10^{12}\) entries. People watch the loss for swings, or estimate the largest curvature by repeated multiplication (0.5). A step size small enough for the sharpest direction makes slow progress along the flat ones. Momentum and Adam (B5) are two methods that help.

Where this is used

Used in: step size and curvature in optimisers (B5), and the Fisher information in B7.

More questions

At a point the gradient is 0 and the curvature is \(-2\). Is it a valley bottom or a hilltop?

A hilltop. Negative curvature means the slope falls as you move, so the loss drops on both sides of the point.

Exercises

Theory

  1. theory The shark weight law is \(W = 4\times10^{-6}L^3\) kg. Find the slope at 50, 80 and 100 cm. By what factor does the slope grow from 50 to 100 cm, and why is it not a factor of 2?

    Hint

    Use the power rule. The slope is proportional to \(L^2\).

  2. theory Show that \(\sigma'(z) = \sigma(z)(1-\sigma(z))\). Write \(\sigma = 1/u\) with \(u = 1 + e^{-z}\), and use the chain rule. Then find the largest value of \(\sigma(1-\sigma)\).

    Hint

    The slope of \(1/u\) is \(-1/u^2\), and the slope of \(e^{-z}\) is \(-e^{-z}\). Note that \(e^{-z}/u = 1 - 1/u\).

  3. theory For \(L(w_1, w_2) = w_1^2 + 3w_2^2\), find the gradient at \((2, 1)\), the direction of steepest descent, and the slope in the direction \((1, 0)\). Which of the two is larger, and why?

  4. theory A chain is \(z = 3x - 1\), \(a = z^2\), \(\ell = a + 5\). Find \(d\ell/dx\) at \(x = 2\) using the chain rule, then check it by nudging \(x\) to 2.001.

Practice

  1. practice Estimate the slope of \(\sigma(z)\) at \(z = 1\) by nudging with \(h = 1, 0.1, 0.01, \dots, 10^{-12}\). Print the error against the formula. Where is it smallest, and why does it grow again for tiny \(h\)?

    Hint

    Computers store numbers with about 16 digits. Subtracting two nearly equal numbers loses most of them.

  2. practice Use made-up lengths [50, 60, 70, 80, 90] cm and weights [0.5, 0.9, 1.4, 2.0, 2.9] kg. For a line \(\hat W = wL\) and the mean squared error, write the derivative with respect to \(w\) by hand and by nudging, at \(w = 0.02\). Do the two agree?

  3. practice For \(f(w) = \tfrac12 k w^2\) with \(k = 6\), run 20 gradient steps from \(w = 1\) with \(\eta = 0.3, 0.33, 0.35\). Which converge? Compare with \(2/k\).

Think deeper

  1. open A friend says: "The gradient of my SharkCam model's loss is zero, so training is finished." Give at least three situations where this is wrong or misleading. How would you tell them apart with the tools of this chapter?

  2. open You wrote gradient code for a new layer and have no reference to compare with. Design a test. Which step size \(h\) would you use, how would you compare the numbers, and where would the test give false alarms (think of ReLU)?

  3. open Some researchers argued that flat minima generalise better than sharp ones, and others showed that sharpness can be changed without changing what a network computes. Using the SharkCam camera moving from clear to murky water, argue for and against the claim "prefer the flat minimum". What would you measure?

Come back later

Try these after two days and again after a week. Answer first, then open.

The slope of \(\ln x\) is \(1/x\). A model gives probability 0.01 to the correct answer and its loss is \(-\ln p\). What is the slope of the loss with respect to \(p\), and what does it say about confident mistakes? (This question uses this chapter and chapter 0.3.)

The loss \(-\ln p\) has slope \(-1/p = -100\) at \(p = 0.01\). The loss is very sensitive to \(p\) there, so a confidently wrong model gets a strong push to raise the probability of the right answer.

A gradient is \((3, 4)\). What is the slope in the direction \((1, 0)\), and which operation from 0.5 gives the slope in any direction?

The slope is 3. The dot product of the gradient with a unit vector gives the slope in that direction. The steepest slope, 5, is the length of the gradient.

Why does a flat sigmoid tail make learning slow? Name the two ideas from this chapter that your answer uses.

The sigmoid's slope is near zero in its tails. By the chain rule, the gradient at an earlier weight includes that slope as a factor, so the product is small unless another factor is large (log loss at the output cancels it, see logistic regression).

  3. Karpathy, A. micrograd, a small library that applies the chain rule automatically over a graph of scalar values. The model for the backpropagation figure in B4. github.com/karpathy/micrograd
  4. Hochreiter, S. and Schmidhuber, J. (1997). Flat minima. Neural Computation, 9(1), 1–42. doi:10.1162/neco.1997.9.1.1. An early argument that a wide, flat region of low loss tends to generalise better than a narrow one.
  5. Keskar, N. S., Mudigere, D., Nocedal, J., Smelyanskiy, M. and Tang, P. T. P. (2017). On large-batch training for deep learning: generalization gap and sharp minima. ICLR 2017. arXiv:1609.04836
  6. Dinh, L., Pascanu, R., Bengio, S. and Bengio, Y. (2017). Sharp minima can generalize for deep nets. Proceedings of the 34th International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2017), PMLR 70, 1019–1028. arXiv:1703.04933. Argues that the sharpness of a minimum depends on how the weights are parameterised.
